name: Mars Surveyor Program
short_status: Two of the four spacecraft flown worked, Mars Global Surveyor and the orbiter renamed 2001 Mars Odyssey; Mars Climate Orbiter and Mars Polar Lander were both lost in 1999. NASA replaced the programme on 26 October 2000.
tagline: NASA · United States · Programme · 1993 · The losing decade Partial

facts.label: What it was, in NASA's own words
facts.value: "In 1994, NASA created a program to send spacecraft to the planet during each launch opportunity every 26 months over the next decade. The first spacecraft under the program, Mars Global Surveyor, was launched in 1996 and is currently in orbit at the planet." That is the description NASA published in its own December 1998 press kit, shortly before Mars Climate Orbiter left Earth.

facts.label: Why it existed
facts.value: Mars Observer, launched 25 September 1992, was lost just before Mars arrival on 22 August 1993 UTC (still 21 August in Pasadena), taking its whole science payload with it. The Surveyor programme was assembled to fly that science again in pieces. The same 1998 press kit records that between them Mars Global Surveyor and Mars Climate Orbiter carried all but one instrument of the entire Mars Observer suite, and that Mars Climate Orbiter's radiometer was a copy of the Mars Observer sounder.

facts.label: One contractor, one operations office
facts.value: "In order to save costs, a single industrial partner, Lockheed Martin Astronautics, was chosen to build and operate all of the Mars Surveyor spacecraft over several years. In addition, an ongoing project office called the Mars Surveyor Operations Project was created at JPL, consolidating management of mission operations across the multi-year program." Both decisions were later examined by the review boards.

facts.label: Faster, Better, Cheaper
facts.value: The doctrine predates the programme. The Mars Program Independent Assessment Team traces it to a speech Daniel S. Goldin gave to JPL employees on 28 May 1992, about two months after he became NASA Administrator, and prints the line on a chart: "...tell us how we can implement our missions in a more cost-effective manner. How can we do everything better, faster, cheaper, without compromising safety?" The team notes that safety, in that context, means mission success.

facts.label: Who managed it, and when that changed
facts.value: JPL created a Mars Program Office in 1994, reporting directly to the Laboratory Director. In 1996 the NASA Administrator moved programme management responsibility from Headquarters to the field centres, and JPL replaced the office with a Mars Exploration Directorate. After Mars Climate Orbiter and Mars Polar Lander launched, that directorate was folded into the much larger Space and Earth Sciences Programs Directorate, where the review team found the Mars Surveyor 2001 project office sitting at the third level, alongside 68 other units of equivalent rank.

facts.label: Three architectures in five years
facts.value: Architecture 1, defined in the autumn of 1995, was a series of modest landers and orbiters on small launch vehicles, with sample return only as an out-year possibility. The announcement of possible fossils in the meteorite ALH84001 in August 1996 changed that. Architecture 2, undertaken in the summer of 1998, promised a Mars sample returned to Earth by 2008, largely through French participation. Architecture 3 was still being drafted when the review team reported in March 2000.

facts.label: What actually flew
facts.value: Four spacecraft. Mars Global Surveyor, launched 7 November 1996, which mapped Mars into 2006. Mars Climate Orbiter, launched 11 December 1998, lost at Mars orbit insertion on 23 September 1999. Mars Polar Lander, launched 3 January 1999, lost during descent on 3 December 1999. And the Mars Surveyor 2001 Orbiter, renamed 2001 Mars Odyssey before launch on 7 April 2001. A fifth spacecraft, the Mars Surveyor 2001 Lander, was built and cancelled.

facts.label: The money
facts.value: NASA's own 1998 press kit prices the two-spacecraft Mars Surveyor '98 project at 193.1 million dollars for spacecraft development and 42.8 million for mission operations, "total $235.9 million for both orbiter and lander (not including launch vehicles or Deep Space 2)." That is one figure covering an orbiter and a lander, which is why single-mission dollar figures quoted for either of them are unreliable.

facts.label: The underfunding finding
facts.value: "In effect, the Mars '98 project attempted to deliver two spacecraft for the price of a Pathfinder. If efficiencies from shared development and operations are factored in, it appears that the Mars '98 project was underfunded by at least 30 percent." The Mars Program Independent Assessment Team, 14 March 2000. Its accompanying chart compares development cost only, in 1999 dollars, excluding launch and operations, and shows Mars Climate Orbiter and Mars Polar Lander each below Mars Pathfinder's bar.

facts.label: The overconstrained box
facts.value: The review team drew Mars Surveyor '98 as a box with schedule, cost, science and launch vehicle all fixed and margins inadequate. "The only remaining variable was risk. Accordingly, project management was faced with managing excessive risk." It also found that the number of flight projects at JPL had gone from two large ones to more than a dozen small ones in about three years, filled by capable but inexperienced project managers with little mentoring.

facts.label: Four reports
facts.value: The Mars Climate Orbiter Mishap Investigation Board Phase I report, 10 November 1999. The same board's report on project management in NASA, 13 March 2000. The Mars Program Independent Assessment Team report, 14 March 2000, chaired by Thomas Young with Kurt Lindstrom as executive secretary. And the Report on the Loss of the Mars Polar Lander and Deep Space 2 Missions, chaired by John Casani, 22 March 2000. The second was released on 13 March 2000, and the last two were made public together at a NASA Headquarters news conference on 28 March 2000.

facts.label: What the review team did NOT say
facts.value: It did not condemn Faster, Better, Cheaper. Having found no established definition, it wrote one, then concluded that FBC "was reviewed extensively by the MPIAT and found to be an effective concept for guiding program implementation, if properly applied" and "should continue to be the approach utilized in the future Mars Program." It also recorded that of the missions studied, none of the failures was the result of new technology.

facts.label: What was said out loud
facts.value: At the 28 March 2000 news conference, NASA Associate Administrator Ed Weiler said of the two 1999 spacecraft: "They both failed. We found the boundary," and "We found the boundary and we're stepping back from that boundary." Administrator Daniel Goldin said "Not one employee is going to be fired." CBS News reported the same day that NASA had said the 2001 lander was cancelled and on hold indefinitely.

facts.label: What replaced it
facts.value: NASA release 00-171, 26 October 2000, announced a Mars Exploration Program developed over the preceding six months: 2001 Mars Odyssey, twin rovers in 2003, a reconnaissance orbiter in 2005, a mobile science laboratory and a first competitively selected Scout mission from 2007, and sample return launches proposed for 2014 and 2016. Scott Hubbard had been installed as Mars Program Director at NASA Headquarters, a post the reviews had demanded. Weiler's phrase in the release was "follow the water."

facts.label: What survived it
facts.value: The programme's last flown spacecraft outlived the programme by a quarter of a century. NASA's Odyssey mission page, last updated 22 June 2026, describes the orbiter as an active mission still studying clouds, fog and frost and mapping surface rocks. Its cancelled sibling, the Mars Surveyor 2001 lander, reached Mars in 2008 as Phoenix.

timeline: Mars Observer, launched on 25 September 1992, is lost just before Mars arrival (21 August in California). The United States has no working Mars spacecraft and no Mars programme.

NASA creates the Mars Surveyor Program to send spacecraft at every 26-month launch opportunity for a decade, with Lockheed Martin Astronautics as sole builder. JPL creates a Mars Program Office reporting directly to the Laboratory Director.
Architecture 1 is defined: modest landers and orbiters on small launch vehicles, with sample return only as a distant possibility outside the planning horizon.

The ALH84001 meteorite announcement lifts public interest in Mars sharply and brings a wave of new requirements, including robotic work tied to the long-term needs of human exploration, managed by a different part of NASA Headquarters. The same year, programme management authority moves from Headquarters to the field centres.
Mars Global Surveyor launches, the first spacecraft of the programme, and goes on to map Mars for a decade.
Architecture 2 responds to the demand for an accelerated sample return, promising Martian samples on Earth by 2008 with substantial French participation.
Mars Climate Orbiter and Mars Polar Lander launch three weeks apart, two spacecraft built for 235.9 million dollars together excluding launch vehicles.
Mars Climate Orbiter is lost at orbit insertion, after a ground software file reported thruster impulse in pound-force seconds instead of the specified newton-seconds.
Mars Polar Lander enters the atmosphere carrying no descent telemetry, by project decision, and is never heard from again. The probable cause is a spurious touchdown signal latched at leg deployment.

The Mars Program Independent Assessment Team delivers its final report to the NASA Administrator, having begun work in early January 2000 and run fact-finding trips to JPL, Lockheed Martin Astronautics in Denver and NASA Headquarters between 11 January and 9 February. It records that NASA has already decided not to fly the Mars '01 lander in 2001 and concurs.

The reports are presented at NASA Headquarters. Weiler says NASA found the boundary and is stepping back from it; Goldin says nobody will be fired; CBS News reports that NASA said that day the 2001 lander has been cancelled and is on hold indefinitely.

NASA release 00-171 announces the Mars Exploration Program: Odyssey in 2001, twin rovers in 2003, a reconnaissance orbiter in 2005, a mobile laboratory and the first Scout from 2007, sample return proposed for 2014 and 2016. The Mars Surveyor Program is over.

images.caption: A colour photograph taken in the Payload Hazardous Servicing Facility at Kennedy Space Center on 19 August 1996, showing the Mars Orbiter Camera being lowered on a crane towards the Mars Global Surveyor spacecraft while gowned technicians on a work platform guide it into place and others watch from the floor. NASA's caption records the camera as one of a suite of six instruments and gives the launch period as opening 6 November 1996.

A colour photograph of 14 September 1998 showing Mars Climate Orbiter suspended on a crane above its opened shipping container in the Spacecraft Assembly and Encapsulation Facility 2 at Kennedy Space Center. The blanketed spacecraft box carries the NASA meatball, a Lockheed Martin logo and a JPL logo side by side, and the container below it is stencilled with the Mars Surveyor '98 triangular mission patch and the words Mars '98 Orbiter.

A colour photograph of 22 October 1998 showing Mars Polar Lander on its workstand in the Spacecraft Assembly and Encapsulation Facility 2 at Kennedy Space Center during testing of the science instruments and spacecraft subsystems. The gold-blanketed lander deck, the stowed solar panels, the three landing legs and the white conical backshell above the deck are all visible, with one gowned technician working on the deck from a step platform.

A colour photograph of a Boeing Delta II lifting off from Launch Complex 17A at Cape Canaveral Air Station with Mars Climate Orbiter aboard at 1:45:51 p.m. EST on 11 December 1998. NASA's caption notes that the launch had slipped one day after a battery-related software problem was found in the spacecraft, and describes the orbiter as the first of the two Mars Surveyor '98 spacecraft.

A colour photograph of 13 March 2001 showing the 2001 Mars Odyssey orbiter in the Spacecraft Assembly and Encapsulation Facility 2 at Kennedy Space Center with the three panels of its solar array opened out ahead of illumination testing, the gold-blanketed spacecraft bus and high-gain dish behind the array, and eight gowned workers standing around it. NASA's caption lists its three instruments as THEMIS, the Gamma Ray Spectrometer and MARIE, and gives the launch date as 7 April 2001.
